mentions_careers.text: Employers increasingly expect graduates to work effectively with AI-assisted development tools.
Preparing students for an industry reshaped by AI is a priority for the department.
Fluency with AI tools is becoming an important skill for careers in software.
Internship partners report that AI-assisted coding is now part of everyday engineering work.
Graduates will enter a job market where working with AI is a baseline expectation.
Our advisory board of industry leaders recommended more practice with AI tools.
Recruiters tell us they look for candidates who know how to direct AI coding tools.
Being productive with AI is quickly becoming part of what a software job requires.
Alumni working in tech say AI assistants changed their day-to-day work.

mentions_collaboration.text: Students are encouraged to treat AI tools as collaborators and to discuss their use openly with peers and instructors.
Faculty and students are working together to explore how AI assistants can support teamwork.
Several courses pair students with AI assistants in collaborative problem-solving exercises.
AI tools can act as a teammate in group projects, alongside human partners.
Instructors and students are co-designing course activities that use AI assistants.
Group assignments may ask teams to decide together how an AI assistant contributes.
Think of the assistant as one more member of your project group.
Students and staff are jointly piloting new ways to work with AI in labs.
Pair programming exercises now include an AI partner alongside a classmate.

mentions_integrity.text: Submitting AI-generated work as one's own is a violation of the academic integrity policy.
Undisclosed use of AI tools will be handled under the honor code.
Students remain responsible for the originality of their work and must not misrepresent AI output as their own.
Presenting a chatbot's answer as personal work counts as academic dishonesty.
Suspected misuse of AI will be referred to the office of student conduct.
Plagiarism rules apply to text and code produced by AI systems.
Passing off machine-written code as your own is treated like any other form of cheating.
Cases where AI output is turned in without credit go through the misconduct process.
Honesty about where each line of code came from is expected of every student.

neutral.text: This guidance applies to undergraduate and graduate courses offered by the department.
The guidance will be reviewed at the end of each academic year.
Questions about this guidance can be directed to the director of undergraduate studies.
A faculty working group prepared this statement after consulting students and staff.
Further details appear on the department's teaching resources page.
Course staff will explain how this guidance applies during the first week of classes.
This page replaces earlier guidance issued by the department.
Updates will be announced on the department's mailing list.
Generative AI tools are changing quickly, and this page will be updated as they evolve.
Many students already have access to AI assistants through campus software licenses.
The department is collecting data on how AI tools are used in its courses.
A survey of AI use among computing students is planned for next year.
Large language models such as chat assistants generate text and code from prompts.
A campus-wide committee on artificial intelligence is reviewing these questions.
Course pages explain how to protect data integrity when submitting files.
This page was prepared in collaboration with the campus library.
The department's teaching collaborative meets monthly to review the curriculum.
Lab machines run regular integrity checks on installed software.

-1.text: The department urges caution with generative AI, and its use is limited to what an instructor explicitly allows.
Generative AI tools raise serious concerns, and students should assume they are not allowed unless told otherwise.
The faculty view AI assistants with caution and restrict them in most courses.
AI assistants are not permitted by default; any use needs an instructor's approval.
Students should generally avoid AI tools unless an instructor indicates otherwise.
Limited use of AI for looking up concepts may be acceptable, but writing code with it usually is not.
We are wary of chatbots in the classroom and allow them only in narrow, instructor-approved ways.
Outside a few clearly marked exercises, AI help is off-limits for now.
It is probably best for students to steer clear of AI tools unless a course explicitly invites them.

-2.text: The department prohibits the use of generative AI tools on any graded work.
Use of AI code generators or chatbots on coursework is not permitted in computer science courses.
Students may not use generative AI systems to complete assignments, projects, or exams.
AI assistants are banned from all programming assignments and exams in the major.
No form of AI assistance is acceptable on graded coursework.
Work produced with the help of an AI model will receive no credit.
Generative models have no place in how our students complete their coursework.
Relying on a chatbot for any part of an assignment is forbidden.
Under no circumstances should students submit work that an AI system helped produce.

0.text: Each instructor sets the policy on generative AI tools for their own course.
The department has not adopted a single rule on AI tools; course syllabi state what is allowed.
Expectations for using AI assistants vary by course and are described in each syllabus.
Whether AI tools may be used is a decision left to individual faculty members.
The department neither endorses nor bans generative AI; course policies differ.
Students should check each course's syllabus, since rules on AI assistance differ between classes.
There is no department-wide position on AI; what applies depends on the class.
AI rules are set course by course, and the department does not override them.
Faculty decide for themselves how, or whether, chatbots fit their teaching.

1.text: The department supports thoughtful use of generative AI tools when students disclose how they used them.
Students are welcome to use AI assistants in many courses, provided they follow the course guidelines.
Generative AI can support learning, and the faculty are adopting it in a growing number of courses.
AI use is not prohibited; students may use these tools as long as they cite them.
In most courses, students may use AI tools for some tasks, subject to instructor guidance.
Responsible use of AI assistants is allowed and, where appropriate, encouraged.
We are not against AI tools; used openly, they can help students learn.
Chatbots are fair game in many classes, as long as students are upfront about it.
Students can likely use AI help in most assignments if they note where it was used.

2.text: The department embraces generative AI as a core part of how computing is taught and practiced.
We are integrating AI coding assistants throughout the curriculum and expect students to use them well.
Generative AI is transforming software development, and our courses are built to put it to work.
We do not see AI as a threat to learning; it is a tool every student is expected to master.
Every computing course now includes assignments designed around AI assistants.
Working with AI tools is a required part of our programming courses.
Far from banning chatbots, our curriculum makes them central to how students build software.
AI pair programming is woven into nearly every course we teach.
Students here learn to program alongside AI from their very first course.

statement_split.rule: A statement is held-out if the numeric part of its inst_id is odd (I001, I003, ...), dev otherwise.

planted_effects.DATA-06: Intro courses are more restrictive than upper-level courses: policy_model.level_effect intro -0.7 vs upper +0.5 (difference 1.2 on the latent scale).
planted_effects.DATA-07: SE courses are more permissive than non-SE courses at the same level: policy_model.se_effect +0.6.
planted_effects.DATA-08: Permissiveness rises each term: policy_model.term_effect_per_step +0.2 per term, F23 (0) to F26 (6).
planted_effects.DATA-09: R1 departments have a more positive statement stance: stance_model.carnegie_effect R1 +0.7, R2 +0.25, others 0.
planted_effects.DATA-10: Planted null: policy_model.control_effect is 0.0 for public and private. inst_effect and the rhetoric-gap flags are drawn independently of control.
planted_effects.DATA-11: Statement labels: stance_latent = intercept + carnegie_effect + policy_coupling (1.2) * inst_effect + noise, so stance tracks the institution's course policies (except rhetoric-gap institutions). label_model: integrity more likely at negative stance (-0.15 per stance point), collaboration (+0.12) and careers (+0.10, +0.15 at R1) more likely at positive stance.
planted_effects.DATA-15: Allowed uses: use_model.base gives intro low code_generation (0.10) and testing (0.12); SE courses the highest code_generation and testing (0.75 each); probabilities scale up with policy.
planted_effects.DATA-16: Assessment: assessment_weights by policy. in_class_exams + oral_defense fall from 0.70 at policy 0 to 0.10 at policy 4; process_logs + ai_critique rise from 0.05 to 0.65.
planted_effects.DATA-17: Rhetoric gap: rhetoric_gap_share 0.15 of institutions (institutions[*].rhetoric_gap). enthusiastic_rhetoric_restrictive_courses: inst_effect -1.0, stance_latent +1.5. cautious_rhetoric_permissive_courses: inst_effect +1.0, stance_latent -1.5.
